title: The Unusual Attitude Of Gifted Teachers
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a rare dual mindset held by the most effective teachers, made up of two seemingly contradictory viewpoints that are actually complementary in practice. The first is caring deeply enough about students' long-term future to refuse any strategy that works short-term but doesn't produce lasting change -- explicitly naming false praise, token economies, rewards, lecturing, restorative justice, and PBIS-style approaches as manipulative or ineffective despite feeling good in the moment. The second is genuinely not caring, emotionally, when a student misbehaves, meaning misbehavior doesn't raise stress or provoke a reaction, because responsibility for handling it has been fully delegated to the classroom management plan, applied like a referee. His central argument is that clean, honest accountability is the only thing that produces internal transformation, since it's the only mechanism that leads students to conclude on their own that they are the problem and only they can fix it, and that combining deep care with emotional detachment produces real authority in the classroom.
points: Effective teachers hold two seemingly contradictory views at once: caring intensely about long-term outcomes while not caring emotionally about individual misbehavior.
A long list of common strategies -- token economies, restorative justice, false praise, PBIS -- are named as short-term, manipulative, or ultimately ineffective.
Accountability is described as the only mechanism that produces true internal transformation, because it forces students to conclude, unprompted, that they are the problem.
Emotional detachment from misbehavior is achieved by shifting full responsibility to a classroom management plan followed like a referee's rulebook.
quotes: There is an attitude gifted teachers carry with them every day of the school year. It’s extremely rare.
This attitude is comprised of two deeply held viewpoints. At first glance, these viewpoints appear contrasting, even impossible to hold at the same time.
All of the above are short-term, external, feel-good, manipulative, and/or don’t change behavior.

Accountability. Clean, honest, undeniable accountability is the only thing in the classroom that changes behavior. It’s the only thing that makes an impact internally, where actual transformation occurs.
No matter what happens from opening bell to dismissal, therefore, you’re as calm and cool as an Artemis astronaut. Mentally untouchable.
The unusual attitude of gifted teachers is to care enough to do what is best for students long-term (accountability), yet not care one whit if a student breaks a rule.
